criterion_notes.c1: Examines household lack of access to piped drinking water in dwellings across municipalities and alcaldías of the Metropolitan Zone of the Valley of Mexico (ZMVM) as well as municipal water supply shortages and tanker truck (pipas) distribution in Ecatepec.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, this paper PASSES (yes) because it discusses water governance (gobernanza del agua), intergovernmental institutional relations (federal, State of Mexico, CDMX, CAEM, SAPASE, and 1983 municipalization/decentralization), and partisan electoral clientelism in municipal water distribution. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, it FAILS (no -> E03) because it does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, formal administrative discretion or accommodation, regulatory enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing access). Instead, its water-access data analysis (Figures 1-2) examines spatial/territorial center-periphery location across concentric urban rings, while its political sections examine macro-governance intergovernmental politics and informal electoral protest/clientelist dynamics. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the paper lacks an identifiable empirical study design linking any governance exposure to a service-access outcome (c5 = no, c3 = unclear).
criterion_notes.c3: Methodologically unclear/borderline: the article contains no methods section and relies on narrative synthesis of secondary literature (e.g., Hernández 2015; Pineda 2002; Perló & González 2009) for its governance claims, although it presents a descriptive map of secondary 2015 INEGI Intercensal municipal piped-water data (Figure 2) and an undocumented hemerographic log of 7 water-related protests in Ecatepec from 2018-2020 (Table 1, with no newspapers, search terms, or selection criteria reported).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports municipal-level percentages of the population without piped water availability inside dwellings (Figure 2, from 2015 INEGI Intercensal data) and describes municipal water supply interruptions and reliance on tanker trucks (pipas) in Ecatepec.
criterion_notes.c5: Does not provide an identifiable empirical study design linking a governance exposure to a service-access outcome: no methods section is reported, Figure 2 compares municipal piped-water lack of access only across geographic concentric rings (spatial periphery, replicating González 2017) with no governance variable, and Table 1 lists 7 protest events from unnamed media sources to examine which level of government residents protest against rather than measuring household or community access outcomes across an identifiable governance exposure.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with trilingual Spanish, English, and Portuguese title, abstract, and keywords); per Criterion 10, direct assessment/translation from the provided Spanish full text is feasible and performed here.

raw_response.exposure: Territorial marginalization and peripheral spatial location across concentric urban rings (Contornos 1-4 vs. Región Central), historical center-periphery inter-basin water transfers (Lerma and Cutzamala), macro-level intergovernmental centralization/municipalization, and partisan electoral clientelism
raw_response.outcome: Municipal share of population without piped water availability in dwellings (INEGI 2015) and water-shortage social protest events/targets in Ecatepec (2018-2020)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Municipalities and alcaldías of the Metropolitan Zone of the Valley of Mexico (ZMVM; 20,892,724 inhabitants across 16 Distrito Federal/CDMX delegations, 59 State of Mexico municipalities, and 1 Hidalgo municipality in 2015 INEGI Intercensal data) and case study of Ecatepec, State of Mexico (1.645 million inhabitants; 7 protest events in 2018-2020)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the article examines lack of household piped water access in the Metropolitan Zone of the Valley of Mexico (c1 = yes, c4 = yes), it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading (c2 = no): its empirical water-access mapping (Figures 1-2, using 2015 INEGI Intercensal data) analyzes spatial center-periphery location across concentric urban rings rather than any legal or administrative rule, and its political sections discuss macro-governance intergovernmental tensions, broad historical municipalization background, and partisan protest/clientelist dynamics rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Furthermore, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2 (where broad governance/clientelism discussion would pass c2), the paper still fails inclusion (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it reports no methods section and provides no identifiable empirical study design linking a governance exposure to a service-access outcome (c3 = unclear, c5 = no; Table 1 compiles 7 unsourced protest events to examine protest targets, while governance claims rely on secondary literature).
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive spatial census mapping and qualitative neoinstitutional/hemerographic case study (no formal methods section reported)
